title: Cause, reason, purpose and result
subtitle: due to, spark off, with the aim of, as a consequence
summary: Say why something happened and what it led to, using the formal cause-and-result vocabulary of written English.

lesson.heading: Cause and reason
lesson.text: Besides *because*, *since* and *as*, there are several noun and verb patterns for causes. Notice which word takes which structure.

examples.text: The collision was **due to** the icy conditions.
The collision was **caused by** ice on the road.
The **cause of** the collision was ice on the road.
The heavy rain **caused** the river **to** flood.
**Owing to** the icy conditions, the two cars collided.

lesson.note: With a clause, owing to must be followed by the fact that: Owing to the fact that the conditions were icy, the two cars collided.

lesson.heading: Formal 'cause' verbs and their typical contexts
rows: The rise in prices **sparked off** a lot of political protest.
The President's statement **provoked** a lot of criticism.
The new law has **brought about** great changes in education.
the direct origins of events and states
This problem **stems from** the inflation of recent years.
The court case **arose from** allegations made in a newspaper.

lesson.heading: Reasons for doing things
lesson.text: To give the reason behind an action, use **reason for** + -ing or **the reason (why) ... was that**. **On the grounds that** introduces a stated justification and is quite formal.

examples.text: Her **reason for** not going with us was that she had no money.
The **reason why** she didn't go with us was that she had no money.
He refused to answer **on the grounds that** his lawyer wasn't there.
I wonder what **prompted** her to send that message?

lesson.heading: Purposes
lesson.text: These are fairly formal and mostly written. **With a view to** sounds a little more indirect than **with the aim of**. Both are followed by -ing.

examples.text: She wrote to the press **with the aim of** exposing the scandal.
I've invited you here **with a view to** resolving our differences.
The **purpose of** her visit was to inspect the equipment.
I wonder what his **motives** were **in** sending that email?

lesson.heading: Results
lesson.text: **As a result** and **consequently** link a cause to what followed; the *consequence* words sound more formal. Note the verb pattern **result in** + -ing.

examples.text: He did no work. **As a result**, he failed his exams.
He did no work. **Consequently**, he failed his exams.
examples.note: more formal than as a result

examples.text: The **result of** all these changes is that no one is happy any more.
His remarks **resulted in** everyone getting angry.

lesson.heading: Result nouns and one very formal verb
rows: the result of a process, or of meetings and discussions
the same idea, but less formal than outcome
the result, seen as what follows on from a cause (formal)
follow as a result; very formal: When the results were announced, chaos **ensued**.

lesson.text: Watch the prepositions: result in, arise from, stem from, give rise to, the purpose of, with the aim of, reasons for.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with the idea it carries.

pairs.right: cause a very strong, perhaps violent reaction
the result of a process or discussion
giving this as the stated reason

exercises.prompt: My reasons ___ not joining the club are personal.
The purpose ___ this pedal is to control the speed.
His stupidity has resulted ___ everyone having to do more work.
All this arose ___ one small mistake we made.
exercises.explanation: arise from / arise out of something.

exercises.prompt: That press article has given rise ___ a lot of criticism.
I came here with the aim ___ resolving our dispute.
exercises.explanation: with the aim of + -ing; compare with a view to + -ing.

exercises.prompt: The train crash was ___ the failure of the electrical system.
exercises.explanation: was due to / was caused by + the cause.

exercises.prompt: The food shortages ___ bad economic policies.
exercises.hint: (s... f... - had their direct origins in)
exercises.explanation: Stem from and arise from explain the direct origins of a state of affairs.

exercises.prompt: The closure of 20 mines ___ strikes in the coal industry. Which verb suits a strong, angry reaction best?
exercises.explanation: Spark off is used for very strong, perhaps violent reactions to events.

exercises.prompt: Join the two ideas: 'The service was terribly slow.' + 'All the customers got angry.'
options: The service was terribly slow. As a result, all the customers got angry.
The service was terribly slow. With the aim of all the customers got angry.
The service was terribly slow. On the grounds that all the customers got angry.
The service was terribly slow. Owing to all the customers got angry.
exercises.explanation: As a result (or the more formal Consequently) introduces the result.

exercises.statement: Owing to the conditions were icy, the two cars collided.
exercises.explanation: Owing to the fact that the conditions were icy, the two cars collided. Owing to needs the fact that before a clause.

exercises.prompt: Join with 'prompt': 'There was a controversial decision. She wrote to the local newspaper to protest.'
exercises.answer: The controversial decision prompted her to write to the local newspaper to protest.
exercises.explanation: prompt someone to do something = be the reason that makes them do it.

exercises.prompt: Does each word introduce a cause, a purpose, or a result?
